Water School Africa (WSA)

Water Literacy Action Methods Hubs

Water Literacy

Water School Africa (WSA) is a partnership between communities engaged in natural water retention practices in their local villages/areas/regions. As it grows across the continent of Africa, you will find communities and methods rom all the 54 countries from the continent presenting their successful water harvesting stories.

The overall goal of this Pan African Water School is to stimulate community interaction and action to improve an understanding of, and boost capacity in sustainable local, community based water resource management across Africa. And then to share that widely with each other as well as with people and communities across the world.

Hubs

We trust in true partnership and facilitate mutual sharing of an unfiltered learning between communities. The successful methods of water retention are often based in traditional wisdom which becomes a resonant route to amplifying action locally. When a local method is successful, it gets talked about more and other communities find it easy to understand and replicate that success.

WSA partners with local respected and successful NGOs to facilitate water literacy in their communities, as articulated by the communities themselves.

pages.title: Water School India - Water Literacy
pages.content:
Water School India (WSI)

Water Literacy Action Methods Hubs

Water Literacy

Water is not just a resource, but a right, a responsibility, and a shared future.

Water School India (WSI) is built on a simple yet powerful idea: water conservation and livelihood generation must go hand in hand.

Water School India believes meaningful work is deeply rooted in the traditional knowledge and rural wisdom that communities have carried for generations. It believes in conserving water and empowering people with the skills, knowledge, and opportunities to lead change in their own communities. When people have secure and dignified livelihoods, their ability and motivation to protect natural resources grows stronger.

The best solutions come from the ground up. Through the Jal Saheli (Friends of Water) group, WSI places women firmly at the forefront of water leadership, learning and change. The women in the local communities are the teachers, the role models, the change-makers in many of the WSI programs.

Water School India aims to train100,000’s of young people, women, community leaders, who will go back into their villages and towns across nation and turn knowledge into action. From groundwater management to local water planning, from reviving traditional practices to influencing water policy, these water stewards will be equipped to respond to today’s challenges with clarity, right knowledge and commitment.

Water School India is a growing community, a shared purpose, and a collective promise to our planet. Water security isn’t just a hope for the future, but a reality we start building today.

PSSS has also initiated a very powerful project called Jal Sahelis (Friends of Water), where women from the most deprived and backward regions in India, faced with every imaginable obstacle in their path, have taken charge and are bringing water to their villages, alleviating severe drought. Their work and success is a tremendous achievement for the world and a masterclass in determination, persistence and action. They have been applauded and awarded by the President of India too!

pages.title: Water School S. America - Water Literacy
pages.content:
Water School South America

Water Literacy Hubs

Water Literacy

Water School South America began with a promise from the children of Barichara, Colombia.

“Felipe Medina of Origen Circular, Barichara Colombia, contacted The Flow Partnership with tales of dry tributaries in Barichara, wondering what they could do and how they might involve their community.

The story that Felipe told of Barichara is not exceptional. It traces how a once thriving ecosystem, through neglect and miscalculation, has been turned into a water-deprived area without a working waste disposal treatment plant that is reliant on a faraway reservoir to pump water in from outside the region. The traditional methods that used to hold the water have been disregarded, the creeks and springs are dry, and water shortages are now common. The forest has been cut, the land has dried out, and the rainfall has diminished without the trees acting to circulate the moisture in the air. Abundant water on our planet is not a guarantee. There is nothing to stop us from breaking the water cycle anywhere and everywhere if we choose to do so. Through our actions, we can easily, over time, become a dry and dusty planet like Mars, incapable of supporting life. Water presents the same challenge for Felipe Medina in Colombia as it does for Rajendra Singh in India, or Zephaniah Phiri in Africa.”
pages.row2:
“Our goals of learning how to live regeneratively remain largely elusive… this deep [dream] of a life transformation takes time to manifest, after all... But it wasn’t until we walked in the forest with a group of children at play that we began to actually do something about it. And this small step may prove to be all the difference in our lives.” - Joe Brewer

(From “The Language of Water” by Minni Jain and Philip Franses, Synergetic Press 2025)

pages.title: Water School S. America - Hubs
pages.content:
Water School South America

Water Literacy Hubs

Hubs

“What began as children asking about water has evolved into a civic movement, a regenerative methodology, and a territorial prototype — now contributing to a global effort to reimagine humanity's relationship with water.”

Chorreras: Water-School South America Hub

Chorreras, a historical site along the Barichara Creek where generations once learned to swim, is currently being activated as a bioregional learning hub for reconnecting community, water, and territory.

  • Youth Formation: water literacy, tropical dry forest biodiversity, ecological tourism.
  • School-Based Learning: ongoing experiential workshops with children, fostering ecological awareness and participation in restoration.
  • Creek Regeneration Prototyping: biofiltration systems, decentralized treatment, ecological restoration approaches.
  • Civic Mobilization: building a cross-sector movement to protect the watershed and sustain long-term care.

    • Read more here: https://www.origencircular.com/water-school
